cards.text: Friend, this one's heavy, so stay close. Jehu has just struck down Joram king of Israel, and his men have shot Ahaziah king of Judah. Now Jehu looks at Samaria, where Ahab, Joram's father, had seventy sons, and he writes letters to the officials, the elders and the guardians of Ahab's sons.
The letter lays it all out. Your master's sons are with you, and you've got chariots, horses, a fortified city and weapons.

cards.question: With all those chariots and weapons in Samaria, what does Jehu's letter tell the officials to do?

answers.text: Crown the best son and fight for Ahab's house
Send the seventy sons away to Judah
Tear down the walls of their own city

cards.text: Pick your best guy, sit him on the throne, and come fight me? I've been a stamper my whole life, friend, and that is a DARE with a stamp on it.

cards.question: The officials in Samaria take Jehu's dare and get ready to fight him.
The officials are terrified, and they reason, "If ___ kings could not stand against him, how can we?"

cards.text: So the palace administrator, the overseer of the city, the elders and the guardians send Jehu a message: "We are your servants, and we will do whatever you say." Friend, that's the "Sounds great, boss!" reply you send before you even finish reading the email.

cards.question: In that same message to Jehu, what do the officials promise they will NOT do?

answers.text: Write to the king of Judah

cards.text: So Jehu writes a second letter. If you're on my side and you'll obey me, bring the heads of your master's sons to me at Jezreel.

cards.question: Jehu's second letter tells the officials to bring the heads to Jezreel by this time ___.
When Jehu's second letter arrives, the leading men of Samaria do what Jehu says.

cards.text: This is a hard one to read, friend. They kill all seventy of the king's sons and send their heads to Jezreel in baskets, and Jehu orders them piled in two heaps at the entrance of the gate until morning.
The next morning, Jehu goes out and stands before all the people.

cards.question: Standing before all the people, what does Jehu admit he did?

answers.text: Conspired against his master and killed him
Sent his men to burn down Samaria
Broke his promise to the elders

cards.text: Jehu tells the people they're innocent. Then he points at those heaps and asks, "But who killed all these?"

cards.question: Jehu says not a word the LORD spoke against the house of Ahab will fail. Through which servant of His had the LORD promised it?
In Jezreel, Jehu strikes down not only what's left of Ahab's house, but also Ahab's great men, close friends and priests.

cards.text: Then Jehu sets out toward Samaria. At Beth-eked of the Shepherds, he runs into some relatives of Ahaziah king of Judah and asks, "Who are you?"

cards.question: What do Ahaziah's relatives tell Jehu they've come down to do?

answers.text: Greet the sons of the king and the queen mother
Carry King Ahaziah's body back home
Join Jehu on his march to Samaria

cards.text: I think nobody has told these men the news. Jehu orders, "Take them alive."

cards.question: Jehu lets some of Ahaziah's relatives go home to Judah.

cards.text: His men slaughter them at the well of Beth-eked. Forty-two men, and he spares none of them.
Leaving there, Jehu finds Jehonadab son of Rechab coming to meet him. Jehu greets him and asks, "Is your heart as true to mine as my heart is to yours?"

cards.question: Jehonadab tells Jehu that his heart is true.
Jehu asks Jehonadab for his hand. Once Jehonadab gives it, what does Jehu do with him?

answers.text: Helps him up into his chariot
Sends him on ahead to Samaria
Makes him a commander of troops

cards.question: Riding along in his chariot, what does Jehu invite Jehonadab to come and see?

cards.text: When Jehu reaches Samaria, he strikes down everyone belonging to Ahab who remained there, until he has destroyed them.

cards.question: In Samaria, Jehu does this according to the word the LORD had spoken to Elijah.

cards.text: And we'll leave it right there for now. Trust me, friend, Jehu's story isn't finished yet.

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 6 quotes "If ___ kings could not stand against him, how can we?", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: The card states facts from outside the passage: Jehu struck down Joram, and his men shot Ahaziah (2 Kings 9:24, 27). It also calls Ahab Joram's father (2 Kings 3:1). None of these carry a reference. The card cites only 2 Kings 10:1.

rule.text: **References.** Every Bible fact he states carries its reference.

findings.problem: Jehu is the main figure, and this card is the first time he appears in the lesson. The card never says who he is, for example the man just anointed king over Israel (2 Kings 9:6).

rule.text: **New people.** The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: The wrong answer "Tear down the walls of their own city" is absurd next to the other answers. A thoughtful baker would dismiss it at once.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: This card repeats the content of verse 3, which card 3 just asked about and answered. It adds a reaction but moves the passage nowhere, so it works as a recap card.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage.

findings.problem: The card calls Jehu's letter a DARE, which adds a motive the text doesn't state. Card 5's question then builds on that framing ("take Jehu's dare").

rule.text: **Reasons:** He never adds why someone did, said or thought something unless the text says why.

findings.problem: The joke "a DARE with a stamp on it" doesn't click instantly. It's unclear what a stamp on a dare means, so a stranger would say "huh?"

rule.text: It clicks instantly for any adult, with no explaining.

findings.problem: The officials read Jehu's letter and surrender out of terror (10:4-5). The comparison is replying "Sounds great, boss!" before finishing an email, which is careless agreement without reading. The core action doesn't match.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The blank asks the baker to fill in the wording of Jehu's letter ("by this time ___"). Nothing earlier lets the baker reason between tomorrow, next week and next month.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: Stop 2's story cards (1, 5, 6 and 10) are plain retellings with almost no Papa Dorin voice. Stop 2 has no humor at all, even where a moment could carry some without muddying a fact, such as the handshake and chariot ride with Jehonadab. Stop 1 cards 2, 9 and 13 have the same issue.

rule.text: **Short, but not stripped down.** A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The last story card is only the "story isn't over" line and tells no verse. It still cites 2 Kings 10:17.
findings.question: When the last story card is just the "story isn't over" line and tells no verse, what should its verses field cite: the passage's last verse, nothing, or something else?
